lead: This unit is about how multimedia data is represented, stored, compressed and played. You will learn to choose file formats, estimate sizes, explain lossless and lossy compression, and read MPEG standards without confusing them with containers. After it, you can plan a small multimedia file and check whether its audio and video stay in sync.
about: This unit explains how multimedia data is represented, stored and compressed. Chapter 4.1 defines multimedia and its elements. Chapter 4.2 compares text, graphics, images, audio and video as non-temporal and temporal media. Chapter 4.3 covers the hardware and software that capture and play them. Chapters 4.4 and 4.5 classify image, animation, audio and video file formats, including containers and codecs. Chapter 4.6 introduces lossless and lossy compression. Chapter 4.7 applies these ideas to audio and video, including motion compensation. Chapter 4.8 surveys the MPEG family and MPEG-7. Chapter 4.9 closes with synchronization of timed streams.

chapters.idea: Multimedia is the computer-controlled integration of several media types, with interactivity as a defining feature.
chapters.depth: Define multimedia, linear multimedia and interactive multimedia. List elements: text, graphics, images, animation, audio, video and interactivity. Give applications in education, entertainment, advertising, medicine, training and public information kiosks. Some syllabi call the elements 'media types' and call linked interactive multimedia 'hypermedia'. Keep system architecture for Unit 6.

figure.aria: A tree with Multimedia at the root and six branches: Text, Graphics, Audio, Video, Animation and Interactivity.
figure.caption: Multimedia combines several media types; interactivity lets the user control the presentation.

chapters.example: A Chennai railway enquiry kiosk shows a train name in text, a route map as graphics, a 20 s audio announcement, a 15 s video advertisement, a 2 s blinking icon as animation, and a touch button for the next page. List the media elements and state why the kiosk is multimedia. Answer: text, graphics, audio, video, animation and interactivity; the media are integrated under computer control and the user can act on them.
chapters.trap: A video clip alone is not multimedia. The exam wants integration plus computer control; interactivity is often required for 'interactive multimedia'.
chapters.leave: Multimedia system architecture to Unit 6; animation principles to Unit 5; color models to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: Each medium has a digital unit: character code, pixel, vector command, audio sample or video frame.
chapters.depth: Text: ASCII and Unicode, fonts, bitmapped versus outline fonts. Graphics: vector versus raster. Images: pixel grid, resolution, color depth. Audio: sampling rate, bit depth, channels; sampling must be above twice the highest frequency. Video: frame rate, resolution, progressive versus interlaced. Classify text, graphics and images as non-temporal; audio, video and animation as temporal or continuous media. Some syllabi call these 'discrete' and 'continuous' media. Leave color models to Unit 1.

figure.aria: A tree with Media at the root split into Non-temporal media: Text, Graphics, Image; and Temporal media: Audio, Video, Animation.
figure.caption: Non-temporal media have no fixed time axis; temporal media are played over time.

chapters.example: Find the raw size of 1 minute of stereo audio at 44.1 kHz and 16 bits per sample, and of one 640×480 RGB frame with 24 bits per pixel. Then find the data rate at 25 frames/s. Use 1 kB = 1000 B and 1 MB = 10^6 B. Audio: 44,100 × 2 × 2 = 176,400 B/s; × 60 = 10,584,000 B = 10.584 MB. Frame: 640×480×3 = 921,600 B = 0.9216 MB; at 25 fps = 23,040,000 B/s = 23.04 MB/s.
chapters.trap: Audio sample rate is per channel; 44.1 kHz stereo has 88,200 samples per second in total. Do not mix bits and bytes or forget frames per second.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 digital images and sampling; Chapter 4.1 for media elements.
chapters.leave: Compression to 4.6; file formats to 4.4 and 4.5; color models to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: A multimedia system is a layer of authoring software and codecs over operating-system drivers and capture, storage and display hardware.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter. Cover capture devices such as camera, microphone and scanner; storage such as hard disk, SSD and optical disk; display and audio devices; GPU and compression hardware. Software: editors, authoring tools, players, codecs, multimedia APIs and drivers. Mention multimedia I/O technologies such as USB, HDMI and audio interfaces without going into their protocols. Keep it shorter than the file-format chapters.

figure.aria: A four-layer stack from authoring application down through codecs and operating-system drivers to hardware.
figure.caption: Software calls codecs and drivers; hardware captures, stores and presents the media.

chapters.example: A small studio records 1080p30 video at 24 bits per pixel and stereo audio at 48 kHz and 16 bits per sample for 2 hours. Find the raw storage. Use 1 GB = 10^9 B. Video: 1920×1080×3×30 = 186,624,000 B/s; × 7200 s = 1,343,692,800,000 B = 1,343.69 GB. Audio: 48,000×2×2 = 192,000 B/s; × 7200 = 1,382,400,000 B = 1.3824 GB. Total = 1,345.08 GB ≈ 1.345 TB. State one choice: a 2 TB SSD plus a GPU with video encode support.
chapters.trap: Do not treat '1080p30' as a file size. It is 1920×1080 pixels at 30 frames/s. A codec can reduce storage, but the raw rate is calculated from pixels, bytes per pixel and frames per second.
chapters.leave: OS scheduling and network QoS to Unit 6; detailed codec algorithms to 4.7.

chapters.idea: A file format fixes how pixels or drawing commands, color information and metadata are stored, often with compression.
chapters.depth: Cover raster formats BMP, JPEG, GIF, PNG and TIFF; vector format SVG; document formats PDF and PSD; WBMP as a 1-bit format. Animation formats: GIF and APNG. Explain color mode stored (RGB, grayscale, indexed, CMYK for print), alpha transparency, lossless versus lossy, and web versus print resolution. Some syllabi call indexed color 'palette color'. Mention web formats: JPEG, PNG, GIF and SVG. Leave color models RGB, CMY and HSV to Unit 1; leave compression algorithms to 4.6.

figure.aria: A tree of file formats split into still images, with raster and vector branches, and animation formats.
figure.caption: Raster formats store pixels; vector formats store drawing commands; animation formats store frames over time.

chapters.example: A web page needs a 1200×800 photograph and a 200×200 logo with a transparent background. Choose a format for each and give a reason. If the photograph is saved as JPEG at 0.5 byte per pixel, find its file size. Answer: JPEG for the photograph; PNG or SVG for the logo. Photograph: 1200×800 = 960,000 pixels; × 0.5 B = 480,000 B = 480 kB.
chapters.trap: JPEG is for photographs, not line art or text. GIF has at most 256 colors. PNG is lossless, so it is not a smaller JPEG for photos. A file extension does not prove which codec was used.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 raster versus vector graphics and color models; Chapter 4.2 media types.
chapters.leave: JPEG, DCT and LZW details to 4.6; animation techniques to Unit 5; monitor setup to 4.3.

chapters.idea: A container file holds audio and video streams that codecs have compressed; the container is not the codec.
chapters.depth: Audio formats: WAV and AIFF (often PCM), MP3, AAC, FLAC and Ogg Vorbis. Video containers: AVI, MP4, MOV, MKV and WebM; codecs such as H.264 and H.265. Explain sample rate, bit depth, channels, frame rate, resolution, bitrate and variable bitrate. 'Full motion video' means about 24–30 frames/s. Some syllabi call containers 'wrapper formats'. Leave streaming and QoS to Unit 6.

figure.title: Container and codecs
figure.aria: Two source streams, video and audio, pass through separate codecs into a muxer, then an MP4 file, then a player.
figure.caption: A container such as MP4 holds video and audio streams that separate codecs have compressed.

chapters.example: An MP4 file holds H.264 video at 2 Mbps and AAC audio at 128 kbps for a 3-minute video. Find the file size, ignoring container overhead. Use 1 MB = 10^6 B. 3 min = 180 s. Video: 2,000,000×180 = 360,000,000 bits = 45,000,000 B = 45 MB. Audio: 128,000×180 = 23,040,000 bits = 2,880,000 B = 2.88 MB. Total = 47.88 MB.
chapters.trap: MP4 is a container, not a codec. A .mp3 file is audio only. Do not confuse bitrate (bits per second) with sample rate (samples per second).
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.2 audio and video representation; Chapter 4.4 image formats.
chapters.leave: Compression algorithms to 4.6 and 4.7; media streaming to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Compression removes redundancy; lossless methods reconstruct exact data, lossy methods discard detail that is less important to the eye or ear.
chapters.depth: Define data redundancy: spatial, temporal, coding and psychovisual. Give compression ratio = original size ÷ compressed size and saving percentage. Lossless methods: run-length encoding, Huffman coding and LZW. Lossy methods: quantization, discrete cosine transform and perceptual coding. Mention entropy coding as the final lossless stage. Some syllabi call lossy compression 'irreversible compression'. Leave JPEG and MPEG details to 4.7 and 4.8.

figure.aria: A tree with Compression at the root split into Lossless methods RLE, Huffman and LZW, and Lossy methods Quantization, DCT and Perceptual.
figure.caption: Lossless methods keep exact data; lossy methods remove detail that is less important to perception.

chapters.example: Huffman-code the symbols A:45, B:13, C:12, D:16, E:9, F:5. Give the code and average length, and compare with a fixed 3-bit code. Build the tree by combining the two smallest weights. Codes: A=0, B=100, C=110, D=111, E=1010, F=1011. Average = (45×1 + 13×3 + 12×3 + 16×3 + 9×4 + 5×4)/100 = 224/100 = 2.24 bits/symbol. Fixed: 3 bits/symbol = 300 bits. Compression ratio = 300/224 = 1.34; saving = 25.3%.
chapters.trap: A Huffman code must be prefix-free. A compression ratio above 1 means the compressed file is smaller. Lossy compression cannot recover the exact original.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.2 data sizes; Chapters 4.4 and 4.5 formats.
chapters.leave: JPEG and MPEG pipelines to 4.7; standards to 4.8.

chapters.idea: Audio compression uses perceptual masking; video compression adds inter-frame prediction and motion compensation to intra-frame coding.
chapters.depth: Audio: PCM as the baseline; psychoacoustic model, frequency masking, temporal masking, MDCT and quantization in MP3 and AAC. Video: I, P and B frames; group of pictures; motion estimation and motion compensation; motion vectors; DCT and quantization of the residual; entropy coding. Some syllabi call motion compensation 'motion-compensated prediction'. Leave MPEG standard names to 4.8.

figure.title: Video coding with motion compensation
figure.aria: The current frame goes to motion estimation, which searches the reference frame; motion compensation forms a residual, then DCT, quantization and entropy coding produce a bitstream.
figure.caption: Motion estimation finds a match in the reference frame; the coder sends the motion vector and the residual.

chapters.example: A 16×16 macroblock in the current frame matches a block at (x+5, y−3) in the reference frame. Write the motion vector. If each vector component uses 8 bits and the residual after compensation has 40 nonzero coefficients at 6 bits each, find the bits for the block. Ignore headers. Answer: motion vector = (5, −3). Bits = 8 + 8 + 40×6 = 16 + 240 = 256 bits = 32 B. Raw block at 8 bits per pixel = 16×16×8 = 2048 bits = 256 B; ratio = 8:1 before headers.
chapters.trap: The motion vector is a displacement, not the absolute block position. Its sign depends on the direction from current block to reference block. An I-frame does not use motion compensation.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.6 compression basics; Chapter 4.2 audio and video.
chapters.leave: MPEG profiles and levels to 4.8; network delivery to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The MPEG family standardizes compressed audio and video; MPEG-7 standardizes descriptions of multimedia content, not compression.
chapters.depth: MPEG-1: video CD and MP3 audio. MPEG-2: DVD video and digital television. MPEG-4: object-based coding and H.264/AVC. MPEG-7: Multimedia Content Description Interface, with descriptors and description schemes for searching and filtering. Mention MPEG-21 only if needed. Some syllabi call MPEG-7 the 'multimedia content description interface'. Keep it an overview.

figure.aria: A tree with MPEG family at the root and four branches: MPEG-1, MPEG-2, MPEG-4 and MPEG-7.
figure.caption: MPEG-1, MPEG-2 and MPEG-4 standardize compression; MPEG-7 standardizes descriptions of content.

chapters.example: A 1-hour DVD video uses MPEG-2 video at 6 Mbps and audio at 448 kbps. Find the total size. Use 1 GB = 10^9 B. 1 h = 3600 s. Video: 6,000,000×3600 = 21,600,000,000 bits = 2,700,000,000 B = 2.7 GB. Audio: 448,000×3600 = 1,612,800,000 bits = 201,600,000 B = 201.6 MB. Total = 2,901,600,000 B = 2.9016 GB. It fits a 4.7 GB single-layer DVD.
chapters.trap: MPEG-7 does not compress data. MP4 is a container; MPEG-4 is a standard family. MP3 is MPEG-1 Audio Layer III, not MPEG-2 video.
chapters.leave: Content-based retrieval and multimedia databases to Unit 6; detailed MPEG-7 descriptors beyond overview.

chapters.idea: Synchronization keeps timed media at the intended relative times during capture, transmission and presentation.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter. Define intra-stream and inter-stream synchronization, skew, jitter, delay and buffering. Explain presentation intervals and synchronization points. Mention that a scheduler compares timestamps and delays or drops data. Keep network protocols such as RTP and QoS to Unit 6. Use lip sync as the main case.

figure.aria: A timeline with a video bar from 120 to 160 ms and an audio bar from 150 to 190 ms.
figure.caption: The video segment starts at 120 ms and the audio segment at 150 ms; the 30 ms skew is inside the ±80 ms limit.

chapters.example: A video frame has timestamp 120 ms and an audio sample has timestamp 150 ms. The allowed skew is ±80 ms. Find the skew and decide if they are in sync. If the audio timestamp is 230 ms instead, what should the player do? Answer: skew = 150 − 120 = +30 ms; |30| ≤ 80, so they are in sync. For 230 ms, skew = +110 ms; delay the video by 110 ms, or drop/duplicate audio if buffering is not allowed.
chapters.trap: Use the absolute skew for the limit. A positive skew means audio is later than video. Buffering adds delay but reduces jitter; it does not remove a permanent skew by itself.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.2 temporal media; Chapter 4.5 audio and video streams.
chapters.leave: Network QoS, RTP and RSVP to Unit 6; detailed scheduling to Unit 6.
